prompt: Which bonds make up a carbon–carbon triple bond?

choices.text: One sp–sp σ bond and two p–p π bonds

choices.why: Only one σ bond forms along the C–C axis. The other two bonds come from sideways overlap of p orbitals.

choices.text: Two σ bonds and one π bond
choices.why: It is the other way round: one σ bond and two π bonds.

choices.text: One sp2–sp2 σ bond and two p–p π bonds
choices.why: Triple-bond carbons are sp-hybridized, not sp2. Each keeps two unhybridized p orbitals for the two π bonds.

explanation: When two sp-hybridized carbons approach each other, one sp–sp σ bond and two p–p π bonds form. The remaining sp orbital on each carbon bonds to another atom at 180° from the carbon–carbon bond.

prompt: What is the H–C≡C bond angle in acetylene, in degrees?
explanation: The two sp hybrid orbitals of carbon lie at 180° to each other. Each carbon uses one for the C≡C σ bond and the other for its C–H bond, so acetylene is linear, with H–C≡C bond angles of 180°.

prompt: How long is the carbon–carbon triple bond in acetylene, in picometers?
explanation: The C≡C bond is 120 pm long, which makes it the shortest known carbon–carbon bond. At about 965 kJ/mol it is also the strongest.

prompt: According to the section, approximately how strong is the C≡C bond of acetylene, in kJ/mol?
explanation: The C≡C bond strength is approximately 965 kJ/mol (231 kcal/mol), making it the strongest known carbon–carbon bond as well as the shortest (120 pm).

prompt: What does the electrostatic potential map of acetylene show?

choices.text: The π bonds create a negative belt around the molecule
The negative region is concentrated on the hydrogen atoms
choices.why: The electron-rich region comes from the π bonds, which surround the C≡C axis between the carbons.

choices.text: The π electrons lie in a single lobe above the C≡C axis
choices.why: The two π bonds together surround the C≡C axis, making a belt of negative charge all the way around.

choices.text: The molecule is bent, with negative charge at the bend
choices.why: Acetylene is linear, with H–C≡C bond angles of 180°.

explanation: Figure 9.3.1 shows acetylene as a linear molecule, and its electrostatic potential map shows that the π bonds create a negative belt around the molecule.

prompt: What is the product when 1-hexyne reacts with 1 equivalent of HBr in acetic acid?

choices.why: That puts Br on the less substituted carbon. Addition follows Markovnikov's rule: H adds to C1 and Br to C2.
That needs a second equivalent of HBr. With 1 equivalent the reaction can often be stopped at the bromoalkene.
Adding one HBr to a triple bond leaves a double bond, so the product is still unsaturated.

explanation: HBr adds to alkynes with Markovnikov regiochemistry: the halogen goes to the more highly substituted carbon (C2) and hydrogen to the less substituted one (C1). With 1 equivalent the product is 2-bromo-1-hexene; excess HBr carries on to 2,2-dibromohexane.

prompt: What is the product when 1-hexyne reacts with 2 equivalents of HBr?

choices.why: Both HBr molecules add with Markovnikov orientation, so both bromines end up on C2, the more substituted carbon.
That would be non-Markovnikov addition. The bromines go to the more highly substituted carbon, C2.
That is the product of 1 equivalent. An excess of HBr adds again to give a dihalide.

explanation: The first HBr gives 2-bromo-1-hexene. The second also adds with Markovnikov regiochemistry, H to C1 and Br to C2, so both bromines end up on C2: 2,2-dibromohexane, the section's example.

prompt: 3-Hexyne, CH3CH2C≡CCH2CH3, reacts with 1 equivalent of HCl. Which product forms?

choices.why: This isomer has H and Cl on the same side. HX addition normally gives trans H and X, which here is the Z isomer.
That forms only when a second equivalent of HCl adds.
One HCl leaves a double bond in place, so the product is a chloroalkene.

explanation: HCl adds to 3-hexyne with trans stereochemistry of H and Cl, giving (Z)-3-chloro-3-hexene. With H and Cl trans, the Cl on C3 and the ethyl group on C4 (the higher-priority group on each carbon) are on the same side, so the alkene is Z. A second equivalent of HCl gives 3,3-dichlorohexane.

prompt: What is the product when 1-butyne reacts with 1 equivalent of Br2?

choices.why: Br2 adds to alkynes with trans stereochemistry. With the two bromines trans, this alkene is the E isomer.
Br2 adds one bromine to each carbon of the triple bond, C1 and C2.
That forms only when a second equivalent of Br2 adds.

explanation: Bromine adds to 1-butyne with trans stereochemistry, one Br on each alkyne carbon, giving (E)-1,2-dibromo-1-butene. A second equivalent of Br2 gives 1,1,2,2-tetrabromobutane.

prompt: What product forms when 1-pentyne reacts with 2 equivalents of Cl2?

choices.why: That is the product of 1 equivalent of Cl2. The second equivalent adds to the remaining double bond.
That would come from 2 equivalents of HCl. Each Cl2 adds two chlorines and no hydrogen.
Cl2 adds no hydrogen. Two equivalents of Cl2 put four chlorines on C1 and C2.

explanation: Each equivalent of Cl2 adds one chlorine to each alkyne carbon. The first gives 1,2-dichloro-1-pentene, and the second adds to that double bond, leaving two chlorines on C1 and two on C2: 1,1,2,2-tetrachloropentane (Exercise 9.3.1a).

prompt: Cyclopentylacetylene, C5H9C≡CH (a cyclopentane ring bonded to –C≡CH), reacts with 1 equivalent of HBr. What is the product?

choices.why: That is non-Markovnikov orientation. Br goes to the more highly substituted alkyne carbon, the one bonded to the ring.
That needs a second equivalent of HBr.
Adding one HBr to a triple bond leaves a double bond. This product is saturated.

explanation: HBr adds with Markovnikov regiochemistry: H to the terminal CH carbon and Br to the carbon bonded to the ring, which is more highly substituted. One equivalent gives 1-bromo-1-cyclopentylethylene (Exercise 9.3.1b).

prompt: What would you expect when 2-heptyne, CH3C≡CCH2CH2CH2CH2CH3, reacts with 1 equivalent of HBr?

choices.why: Markovnikov's rule can't choose here: each alkyne carbon carries one alkyl group, so Br can add to either one.
Both alkyne carbons are equally substituted (one alkyl group each), so both orientations occur.
Dibromides need a second equivalent of HBr. One equivalent leaves a double bond in place.

explanation: Markovnikov's rule puts the halogen on the more highly substituted alkyne carbon, but in 2-heptyne C2 and C3 each carry one alkyl group. Neither is favored, so Br adds to both, giving 2-bromo-2-heptene and 3-bromo-2-heptene (Exercise 9.3.1c).

prompt: What is the hybridization of the positively charged carbon in a vinylic carbocation?

choices.why: sp2 is the hybridization of the cationic carbon in an alkyl carbocation. The vinylic cation carbon is sp-hybridized.
An sp3 carbon has four groups around it. The vinylic cation carbon is sp-hybridized, with a vacant p orbital.

choices.text: None; it uses only unhybridized p orbitals
choices.why: The cationic carbon is sp-hybridized. Only its vacant orbital is a p orbital.

explanation: A vinylic carbocation has an sp-hybridized carbon. Figure 9.3.2 shows its vacant p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the π bond orbitals. A vinylic carbocation generally forms less readily than an alkyl carbocation.

prompt: How many R groups are attached to the positively charged carbon of a secondary vinylic carbocation?
explanation: Figure 9.3.2 notes that only one R group is attached to the positively charged carbon of a secondary vinylic carbocation, rather than two as in a secondary alkyl carbocation. The cationic carbon's other connection is the double bond.

prompt: According to the section, a secondary vinylic carbocation forms about as readily as which kind of carbocation?

choices.why: Vinylic carbocations generally form less readily than alkyl carbocations. A secondary vinylic one only matches a primary alkyl one.
Vinylic carbocations are harder to form than alkyl carbocations, so a secondary vinylic one comes nowhere near a tertiary alkyl one.
A primary vinylic carbocation is so hard to form that there is no clear evidence it even exists.

explanation: As a rule, a secondary vinylic carbocation forms about as readily as a primary alkyl carbocation, and a primary vinylic carbocation is so difficult to form that there is no clear evidence it exists. That is why many alkyne additions occur through more complex mechanistic pathways.
